reason: The sources provide cross-verified evidence across multiple independent sites regarding VY Canis Majoris's extreme dimensions, historical dimming, mass-loss mechanisms, and stellar fate.
story: In 1801, astronomers recorded the crimson star VY Canis Majoris as a visible point of light. Today, it has faded from human sight, requiring a telescope to observe. What happened? VY Canis Majoris is a red hypergiant 3,900 light-years away and one of the largest stars in the Milky Way. If dropped into our solar system, its monstrous surface would engulf Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and stretch past the orbit of Jupiter. This behemoth churns with violent convective cells, some larger than our entire Sun. These boiling cells blast massive plumes of gas into space. As this expelled material cools, it condenses into thick dust, forming a dense circumstellar shroud that has progressively choked off the star's visible light over the past two centuries. Though less than ten million years old, this bloated giant is nearing the end, destined to either detonate as a supernova or collapse directly into a black hole.
angle: Boiling convection cells on the surface of VY Canis Majoris are larger than our entire Sun, and their violent eruptions have coughed up enough dust to erase the star from human naked-eye visibility over the past two centuries.

claims.claim: VY Canis Majoris is an extreme red hypergiant star located in the constellation Canis Major.
VY Canis Majoris is situated approximately 3,900 light-years away from Earth.
VY Canis Majoris ranks among the largest known stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
If placed at the center of our solar system, VY Canis Majoris would encompass or extend beyond the orbit of Jupiter.
The estimated radius of VY Canis Majoris is approximately 1,420 times that of the Sun.
Astronomers have described the extreme behavior and scale of VY Canis Majoris as 'Betelgeuse on steroids'.
VY Canis Majoris was historically visible to the naked eye but now requires a telescope to be observed.
The star has experienced gradual fading in brightness over the past couple of centuries due to ejected gases forming obscuring dust.
Telescope observations have revealed discrete knots of ejected hot gas near the star that formed less than 100 years ago.
Mass-loss episodes on VY Canis Majoris are driven by large-scale convective cells that can be as large as the entire Sun.
The red hypergiant phase of VY Canis Majoris is estimated to last between 100,000 and 500,000 years.
Despite its immense size and advanced evolutionary state, VY Canis Majoris is less than 10 million years old.
Astronomers predict VY Canis Majoris will end its life as a supernova within the next 100,000 years.
Scientists theorize that VY Canis Majoris could potentially skip the supernova phase entirely and collapse directly into a black hole.
Spectroscopic measurements have identified molecules of water and carbon monoxide within the dense gas clouds surrounding the star.
A controversial 2006 study suggested VY Canis Majoris had an effective temperature of 3,650 Kelvin and a radius of only 600 solar radii.
VY Canis Majoris is physically associated with the massive interstellar molecular cloud Sh 2-310.

disputed: Distance from Earth: S1 and S7 cite roughly 3,900 light-years (1.2 kpc), while S4 cites 4,500 light-years and S3 notes 5,000 light-years. Script should state 'around 3,900 light-years away' based on recent radio parallax measurements.

Radius and solar system extent: Modern consensus puts its radius at 1,420 solar radii (extending past Jupiter, per S1, S2, and S7), whereas older studies estimated 1,800 to over 3,000 solar radii (extending out to Saturn, per S4). Script should specify Jupiter's orbit and attribute larger estimates to historical measurements uncorrected for surrounding dust.

Current and initial mass: Estimates range between 15 to 19 solar masses currently (with an initial mass around 25 to 32) in S1, compared to 20 to 25 currently and 30 to 40 initially in S4, and 30 to 40 in S2. Script should attribute broadly: 'between 15 and 30 times the mass of the Sun'.
Final evolutionary fate: Sources debate whether it will explode as a supernova or collapse directly to a black hole. Script should present both as competing scientific possibilities.
